# Draft:Lyon During the Renaissance (c. 1450–1600)

.]]
The Renaissance in Lyon concerns the history of the city of Lyon during the Renaissance.
It begins in the middle of the 15th century with the establishment of the Fairs of Lyon by the French king Charles VII. This event placed the city at the center of major European commerce and revitalized the former episcopal city. Numerous foreigners, especially Italians, soon settled in the city, which became an important center of Renaissance culture, with significant banking and publishing activities. This era also saw the introduction and early development of the silk industry. During the Wars of Religion, the city experienced a brief Protestant occupation, followed by the Lyonnais vespers, a massacre of Protestants in the wake of the St. Bartholomew's Day massacre. Initially aligned with the Catholic League, Lyon submitted to King Henry IV after his conversion to Catholicism; the king subsequently reformed the consulate to secure the city's loyalty.
The city and its inhabitants
The city along the Rhône experiences significant demographic and urban expansion during the Renaissance. While its boundaries do not expand substantially, it densifies through the raising of buildings and the subdivision of undeveloped areas. Supported by increasing prosperity, numerous stone structures are erected, though no large prestigious public buildings appear.
The most prominent Lyonnais institution is the consulate, which connects with the populace primarily through the pennons for policing duties and the General Alms for welfare. The political landscape is rounded out by the governor and the foreign nations.
Topography and architecture
Driven by sustained prosperity, the city continually develops and rebuilds. Its overall layout remains largely unchanged; rather than sprawling outward, it densifies inward. Gardens gradually shrink, and houses are rebuilt on-site with additional stories. However, the southern part of the Peninsula and the hill slopes remain unurbanized.
Faced with the evolving functions and socio-economic significance of their city, the consulate seeks to adapt a still typically medieval urbanism (narrow streets, few public squares, homogeneous neighborhoods) to new demands. Over the 150 years of the Lyonnais Renaissance, the city's elites successfully transform it: neighborhoods become distinct and specialized, public squares emerge, and key thoroughfares are improved. Nevertheless, they fail to achieve their ambition of glorifying the city with monumental works, as seen in other major European cities of the era.
Morphology of civil buildings
The rise in inhabitants per household coincides with the economic surge beginning around 1460. The right bank of the Saône, in particular, undergoes a wave of demolitions to make way for taller, more opulent structures. Cultivated spaces vanish during this period, and throughout the 16th century, any building capable of being heightened is raised. Until the 1500s, architectural styles draw from Gothic influences, later evolving into a eclectic blend of various elements. The city's wealth enables a renewal of Gothic building art, though the Renaissance style does not become predominant. This intense densification gives rise to traboules—private passages that, by necessity, become semi-public thoroughfares of ambiguous status, used by pedestrians navigating the narrow, congested streets.
Obtaining a comprehensive view of house morphologies from this era is challenging, as even the extensive Old Lyon district features many partially rebuilt structures from later centuries. Generally, buildings are narrow (five to six meters wide) and deep (up to twenty meters), typically with two stories. Many connect to a rear building—sometimes up to four in total (as in the "Grande Traboule")—linked by galleries at each level, accessible via spiral staircases. Alongside these ordinary residences, numerous luxurious homes emerge from the 15th century onward, such as the Maison de la Rose on Rue Mercière, owned by the councilor Ennemond de Syvrieu and later by Jacques Cœur.|group=note}} The grandest residences incorporating Renaissance elements, however, date to the 16th century. These elite homes illustrate the gradual fusion of medieval Gothic with ancient motifs drawn from Italian Renaissance architecture. }}
General evolutions

Despite resistance and the consulate's lack of consistent resources, numerous changes in the urban fabric are evident across four successive phases.
From the mid-15th century to 1500, the city densifies without significant new builds, primarily by elevating existing structures. Prosperity returns in the 1460s, but recovery from the Hundred Years' War takes time. In 1468–1470, the consulate authorizes some constructions on Rue Mercière or at the Saulnerie; concurrently, it contemplates demolishing the Saint-Vincent borough to bolster northern defenses or permits the demolition of an alley to expand the Grandes Carmes cloister. Visible signs of urban evolution include the opening of two Saône ports: Saint-Éloi (1482–1483) and Saint-Paul (1485–1490).
From 1500 to 1540, new builds occupy wastelands and gardens. The city densification eliminates open spaces, resuming the horizontal expansion that had been interrupted since the mid-13th century. Only between 1540 and 1560 does systematic road rationalization begin, accompanied by the creation of new public squares. Finally, from 1560 to 1600, despite some alterations by the Protestant authorities for military circulation on major routes, urban development stabilizes amid political and economic crises that limit resources.
Lyon lacks a political force strong enough to mobilize capital, champion large projects, and overcome opposition—as in Paris or major Italian cities—explaining the absence of monumental civic buildings. Several mid-16th-century proposals made at the peak of prosperity, such as rebuilding Place du Change (the center of Lyonnais business) or erecting a civic palace, are not carried out.
Urban transformations
, 1908.]]
Lyon must accommodate a larger, wealthier population and a massive influx of people and goods four times yearly during the fairs. This adaptation involves conflicts and resistance, with key changes enforced by the Protestant consulate, implementing long-debated measures.
At Fourvière's base, the canons' cloister at Saint-Jean Cathedral is forcibly opened by Baron des Adrets, who razes its walls in 1562. On the Peninsula, convent and church cemeteries become squares: Jacobins (1562), Cordeliers (1567), and Saint-Nizier (1593). The present-day Place Bellecour area serves as military ground, redeveloped multiple times. At Croix-Rousse's foot, the ancient Terreaux ditch is filled to enable urban extension downhill. Similarly, the fortified Saint-Just cloister is dismantled from May to September, though planned since 1525. These efforts—eliminating wall vulnerabilities and creating drill squares—prepare for anticipated conflict.
The traditional traversal axis—Rhône bridge, rues Bourgchanin, Confort, Mercière, and Saône bridge—is duplicated by one via Rhône bridge, Rue de la Barre, Place Bellecour, Port du Roi, Saône ferries, Port des Estres, rues Bombarde and Chemin-Neuf. Other streets are also developed.
From the late 14th century, the consulate pursues a public water policy, securing concessions for religious-controlled sources to augment its own. The oldest public sources—Choulans, Saint-Épipoy, and la Chana—were supplemented in 1396 by fountains at Saint-Marcel, Sainte-Catherine, and des Gardes. In 1504–1506, Choulans sources are partially diverted to supply Saint-Laurent-des-Vignes hospital and three new fountains at la Blancherie, Maison Athanase, and Jardin des Fleur de Lys. By 1530, the city has about fifteen public fountains: twelve on the Saône's right bank and three on the left.
Socio-economic evolutions
Urban activity locations also shift. The main cattle market, sited on Rue Juiverie until 1490 amid an expanding business district, relocates to Place de la Croix de Colle. Similarly, the pig market moves from the center in 1513 to the Lanterne ditches. Slaughterhouses likewise shift early in the 16th century from Saint-Paul and Saint-Nizier to Place de Bourg Neuf and the filled Lanterne ditches. These changes reflect municipal efforts to move polluting activities to the periphery, allowing the center to concentrate on residential use and reducing sources and spread of disease.
The city's neighborhoods
.]]
By the late 15th century, the densest areas are the Saône's right bank and, on the Peninsula, a bourgeois urban core along the era's Rue Mercière (via mercatoria), spanning from Saône to Rhône bridge. Corporations, trades, and foreign nations cluster tightly in neighborhoods or streets, reflecting Lyon's strong social organization.
Saint-Georges, Saint-Jean, and the Roanne palace neighborhood
, 1908.]]
Fourvière's lower slopes are narrow, topography-constrained. Main streets parallel the river, with limited cross-ways. Upper slopes are nearly uninhabited, covered in woods, gardens, and vines.
Saint-Georges is a poor Renaissance neighborhood of affaneurs, fishermen, masons, weavers, and boat builders. Yet it houses the wealthy Bellièvre family and the Order of Saint John of Jerusalem commandery. Its hôtel is built in 1492 by Humbert de Beauvoir, who restores Saint-Georges Church.
The Roanne hôtel, seneschalsy seat since 1435, populates surrounding streets with royal officials. During the Italian Wars, it hosts the king and court. Along Rue du Palais, early Renaissance residents form a solid middle bourgeoisie of merciers, furriers, apothecaries, notaries, changers, and lawyers. As royal influence grows via Roanne, poorer inhabitants shift south toward Saint-Jean and Saint-Georges. In 1538, with Francis I's approval, the consulate demolishes Roanne's enclosure for a square bearing its name.
Poor folk—affaneurs, fishermen, boat builders—cluster around the canonical quarter along Rue de la Bombarde, Rue Tramassac, and Gourguillon. This canonical quarter bisects the Saône's right bank; bypassing its wall requires Rue de la Bombarde to Rue Tramassac. The cloister has gates: one to Roanne palace, Porte Froc to Rue Saint-Jean, another to Rue Tramassac, and one south to Saint-Pierre-le-Vieux Church. The latter, a parish church, features chapels maintained by Lyonnais bourgeoisie for burials, including Bellièvre, Bullioud, and Laurencin.
In the Renaissance, as Louis XI seizes Pierre Scize castle, Archbishop Charles de Bourbon reoccupies the intra-muros palace. He extensively renovates it around 1466 to modernize it, though he resides little in Lyon.
This era also sees completion of Saint-Jean Cathedral with lateral chapels.

Saint-Paul, Pierre-Scize, and Bourgneuf
}}
Between Saint-Paul and Saint-Christophe, armorers, printers, and booksellers thrive. Southern Saint-Paul square hosts many changers, goldsmiths, and merchants of Piedmontese, Florentine, or Spanish origin. This neighborhood's population, poor after the Hundred Years' War, grows wealthier during the 15th century, with menial activities largely disappearing.
Between Rue Juiverie, Place du Change, and Notre-Dame du Palais lies the core of Lyonnais banking and a major commercial center led by Italians and housing clerks from across Europe. In the mid-15th century these streets still housed commoners, who were gradually displaced. Rue Juiverie, for example, initially described as poor and "wide, poorly peopled with Jews and poor folk," became occupied by Italian merchant-bankers who built large houses, turning it into "one of the city's finest" streets.
Pierre-Scize and Bourgneuf long specialized in textile activities and remain relatively poor. In 1561 the consulate razes a gate, four houses, and a tower to create Place de Bourgneuf.

Fourvière plateau, Saint-Just, and Pierre-Scize
Fourvière plateau is sparsely populated, mostly rural. Hill slopes develop only along ascending roads like Montée du Gourguillon or the newly created Chemin-Neuf.
Southward, Saint-Just—juridically separate from Lyon and controlled by the canons—is walled off from the agglomeration. Proximity nevertheless integrates it urbanistically; for example, Saint-Paul's cattle market is relocated there. The separation ends under Protestant rule, when Huguenot authorities demolish the cloister walls.
Northward, the archbishop's former castle of Pierre Scize, now owned by the king and administered by the governor, overlooks the city.
Peninsula: Bellecour to Saint-Vincent slopes
, 1908.]]
Empire-side urbanism is more fragmented than Kingdom-side, due to recent urbanization. It comprises three 9th-century vici: northern Saint-Vincent, central old borough (around Saint-Nizier), southern Bourg Chanin.
Saint-Nizier is this side's commercial hub, facing the Change. centerd on Saint-Nizier Church, completed late 16th century. Surrounding streets house furriers, merciers, drapers, merchants, and notaries on Rues Vendrant, Longue, and Rue Mercière. Bourgeois families such as Humbert, Aynard de Varey, and Humbert de Villeneuve reside there; Rue Mercière alone is home to Le Maistre, Syvrieu, and Thomassin. In the late 15th and early 16th centuries the area specialises in cloth and fur trade and parchment-making; printers become prominent later. The bourgeoisie merges with the nobility through lordships or royal service and includes many Milanese and German residents.
Peripheral streets house better-off artisans and commoners who benefit from the fairs. Rues de la Pêcherie and de l'Erberie—occupied by fish handlers and sellers—are no longer poor districts.
Farther out, toward the Rhône or down to Bellecour, living conditions remain modest.
The current Croix-Rousse slopes, then called Saint-Vincent, are sparsely populated but gradually densify, as does the left bank of the Rhône. Houses are built along the Terreaux fortifications, and the Déserte neighborhood forms at their base. For protection, Louis XII orders an uphill rampart in 1512; the plans and works are directed by Jean Perréal.
Peninsula: Bellecour to Ainay
South of Bellecour, especially from Ainay Basilica, the area consists mainly of meadows, orchards, marshes, and islands. Convents own large agricultural domains there. Renaissance-era urbanization largely bypasses this zone. The 270-meter stone bridge over the Rhône, originally half stone and half wood, is rebuilt entirely in stone between 1559 and 1560 after several collapses.
Demography and immigration
Accurate population estimates are challenging without censuses. Richard Gascon uses tax rolls and house levies to discern trends: population doubles from 1450 to 1500, then again in the early 16th century. This mirrors France's urban growth, with 10–100% increases from late 15th to mid-16th century.
From the 1430s–1440s low, Lyon's population grows steadily. Kleinclausz estimates 25,000 mid-century. Growth accelerates to ~35,000 by 1520 and 50,000–60,000 (or 75,000) mid-century. This increase is primarily driven by immigration from Savoy, Dauphiné, and Burgundy.
The consulate faces difficulties meeting the food requirements created by this growth. Local production proves insufficient, leading to increased imports from Burgundy—one of the causes of the 1529's Grande Rebeyne. Epidemics of plague periodically reduce the population, but immigration rapidly restores numbers. The Wars of Religion cause a marked decline; Zeller estimates 30,000–35,000 inhabitants by the late 16th century.
While Renaissance Lyon is cosmopolitan, most foreigners are transient or short-term residents. Few non-French speakers settle permanently. In the mid-16th century the majority of migrants who married and settled came from Savoy, the County of Burgundy, and Dauphiné; smaller numbers originated in the Lyonnais, nearby Auvergne, or other parts of France; approximately 5% were non-French speakers.
Institutions
.]]
Renaissance Lyon's institutions—civil, military, judicial, religious—overlap, intermingle, clash, or oppose, often without clear boundaries.
The central institution is the consulate, which manages relations with subordinate civil bodies such as the General Alms, the Pennons, and confraternities, as well as with royal authority. Judicial authority initially lies with ecclesiastical courts before gradually passing to royal jurisdiction. Royal power is strongly represented through the governor and the bureau of finances. Foreign merchants exercise influence through formally recognized "Nations" that handle their grievances and defense.
The consulate
Lyon's consulate comprises wealthy merchants from leading families. Charles VIII grants nobility privilege to consuls in 1495.
Consuls' sociological origins evolve: late 15th-century law-men (tied to royal roles) dominate; merchant families rise with prosperity, reducing office-holders to a quarter by 1520–1530, under a fifth 1540–1550, rebounding to majority under Henry IV. Regardless, limited lineages dominate: Regnault, Faure, Henry, Fenoyl, La Porte, ~15 others. Despite biennial renewal, continuity prevails.
Twelve-consul renewal: annual halving in December. Incumbents select two trade masters per guild; assembly elects six notables joining prior six. Cooptation excludes clergy, nobles, commoners.
Daily functioning
Medieval to 1461: routine at consuls' homes, assemblies in Saint-Nizier's Saint-Jacques chapel (nave for crowds). Post-hesitation, Rue Longue's Maison Charnay for about 50 years. 1512 fire damages uppers; the consulate lacks an official venue for many years. 1564: Hôtel de Milan, Rue Grenette/Place des Cordeliers corner. Until 1576, then Rue Longue to 1604. The consulate then purchases the house at the sign of the Couronne, 13 Rue de la Poulaillerie.
Decisions: partial assemblies for routine; full meetings rare. Major issues (especially finances): general assembly (former consuls and key figures, 20–25 people) or trades assembly. The latter theoretically represents economic interests but excludes the general populace, underrepresents newer trades (printers first appear in 1568), and usually defers to notables.
Consular powers
Limited by royal and local powers, the consulate nevertheless possesses substantial authority: it appoints trade and terrier masters (often former échevins or provosts), convenes notables, selects city officers, designates deputies to the Estates General or court, and recruits clerks. In policing it appoints pennon captains and may imprison or exile offenders.
On economic matters it controls 51 trades, records their regulations, and appoints masters. It taxes goods entering the city, ensures conformity of weights and measures, and maintains roads to facilitate circulation.
Administrative personnel
The administrative staff grows and becomes more specialized. From 1506 legal acts are handled by a general prosecutor (a law graduate).
Financial administration (goods duties, octrois, donations, taxes): a treasurer and general receiver exist from the late 14th century; the latter becomes the "receiver of common deniers" in 1543.
The municipal militia
The municipal militia consists of all able-bodied adult males organized by neighborhood, supplemented by professionals paid by the consulate. It is divided into seven banners and approximately thirty pennons, each subdivided into groups of about ten men commanded by dizeniers. Ordinary citizens perform rampart watch duties, while paid professionals guard the city and its gates; the bourgeois elite serve mounted and within the city walls.
Lyon's royal companies
In 1430 the bourgeois militia company distinguishes itself at the Battle of Anthon against the Prince of Orange. In 1431 Charles VII elevates the Lyonnais archers to the status of a Royal Company. The company includes free archers and crossbowmen.
Placed under the patronage of Saint Sebastian, it uses the Saint-Germain chapel in Saint-Nizier church from 1486. Statutes of 1498 establish a second company. Training initially takes place in the Rue Grôlée and Rue de l'Hôpital; from 1513 it moves to the mound of the Auges owned by the company, between the Rues des Augustins and Place Sathonay.
The companies' role declines after the creation in 1498 of a company of culveriniers and arquebusiers; the original royal companies are dissolved in 1591. From 1561 the arquebusiers provide the city guard, consisting of 200 men under a captain appointed by the consulate.
Confraternities
From the early 14th century territorial confraternities dedicated to the Holy Spirit serve as intermediaries between the population and the consulate. Grouped under the Trinity confraternity, these societates or frairies organize neighborhoods through festivals, rituals, and the election of couriers, and the management of hospital, funeral, and festive functions. Usually socially and geographically homogeneous, they contribute to social regulation.
Their principal rivals are the professional confraternities. By 1530 two-thirds of the forty-eight officially recognized confraternities are professional. organized by trade networks rather than territory, they are difficult to locate spatially except for their spiritual seats in churches. These newer, protective associations parade with banners and perform displays of strength, provoking outbreaks of violence that the authorities deplore but prove unable to suppress.
Hospital and assistance institutions
During the Renaissance Lyon possesses numerous shelters for the sick and poor. Most are linked to ecclesiastical institutions and supported by donors; over time they come increasingly under consulate control, culminating in the creation of the General Alms in 1534.
General Alms
, 1539. University of Virginia.]]
Population growth greatly increases the number of poor and needy, overwhelming traditional ecclesiastical charity. The consulate establishes public assistance to cope with the influx and to aid impoverished residents of Lyon. As in Paris, Rouen, and Dijon, rising food prices push many workers into poverty, and the desire to maintain charity and social peace prompts organized relief. The 1529 rebeyne and the 1539 printers' strike encourage the elite to act.
The General Alms is instituted in 1534, following a decision taken after the famine of 1531. Financed by contributions from the bourgeoisie and administered by eight or nine rectors chosen from the consuls, it primarily subsidizes bread. Members sometimes advance funds at personal risk but thereby gain priority for the office of échevin.
The Alms' primary task is assistance: it owns a mill and bakery and, in times of famine, distributes bread to all the poor; in normal periods only to invalids, the sick, widows, and orphans. A secondary aim is to provide work: children are apprenticed to drapers or placed as domestics in notables' households, while adults are employed cleaning ditches and streets. Able-bodied beggars frequently resist forced labor and are sometimes have to be chained or imprisoned for refusal. Police functions become linked to assistance: beadles known as chasse-coquins are appointed to drive away outsiders attracted by the distributions. The coercive aspect of the system produces mixed feelings among recipients.
The institution is created earlier than similar bodies elsewhere in France and fits the broader European trend toward secular and professionalized poor relief. It reflects a changing Western perception of poverty: from the deserving needy to the able-bodied unemployed whose control is necessary for public order. Humanist thought regards extreme poverty as reducing people to an animal state.
In 1560 the General Alms becomes an independent body, a status formalized by letters patent of Charles IX. Rectors are chosen by cooptation, subject to ratification or nomination by the consulate, which retains control over major decisions.
Hospitals
Institutions vary in longevity; some endure for centuries, while others cease operation shortly after their foundation. A precise list is difficult to establish, as the sources are partial, indirect, or imprecise.
Notable examples include:
* The oldest on the Peninsula is the "Rhône Bridge hospital." This medieval "Holy Spirit Almonry," also known as the "poor hospital" or "Alms house," was founded in 1129 by the Holy Spirit confraternity. In 1335 it passed to the Chassagne abbots and was renamed. By 1478 it had been transferred to the consulate. It was located south of the Bourgchanin, near the river.
* On the Mercière-Saône side is the "Saint-Antoine hospital," prominent in the 15th century. The Sainte-Catherine hospital (on the current Rue d'Algérie) was dependent on the dames of Saint-Pierre and received many bequests. There was also a modest "widows' hospital" or Hôtel-Dieu des femmes: mainly for plague victims, on the Mercière, Rues Raisin-Thomassin.
* On the right bank of the Saône are several ancient institutions associated with the parishes of Saint-Georges and Saint-Paul.
* The latter includes the "Two-Lovers hospital" (at the end of Rue Bourgneuf), which replaced "la Chana"; and the "Saint-Eloi hospital" near the church, which disappeared in 1503 following a suit between the chapter and the consulate.
* Saint-Georges had the hospital of the Knights Hospitaller ("Saint John of Jerusalem hospitaliers") for pilgrims. Near Sainte-Marie was a small hospital of the same name. Both were minimally active. In 1474 Jacques Caille and Huguette Balarin founded the "Saint-Laurent hospital" for plague victims, acquiring the Saint-Laurent des vignes chapel of the Saint-Irénée chapter and adjoining buildings, below the parish. It developed and passed to the consulate. The church was undersized; the Trinity confraternity enlarged it in 1509. In 1533 Thomas II de Gadagne, via the Dominican Sante Pagnini, commissioned Salvator Salvatori for a third building.
All were small, with few beds; they mainly served as points for distributing food to the poor. The managing religious orders were often underfunded and relied on lands and legacies; they frequently had to beg to supplement their income.
Leper houses
In the 15th century there were four external houses for plague victims and the sick, banished out of fear of contagion. Near Saint-Irénée: Griffon; Saint-Foy: Saint-Martin; Vaise: Saint-Pierre/Balmont; opposite the Rhône bridge (replacing Béchevelin): Sainte-Madeleine.
Justice
Philip V's 1320 decision vests secular justice solely in the archbishop. This is gradually eroded by the king's bailiff, preferred by bourgeois escaping local ecclesiastical sway. Francis I fully assumes control in 1531; Henry II returns it in 1547. The 1562 Protestant seizure allows the king to illegally seize all judicial powers, with the archbishop absent. This becomes permanent. Post-dating ecclesiastical seigneurial powers: the archbishop's Pierre Scize castle, cathedral chapter's Saint-Jean cloister.
The consulate is never granted judicial powers by the king. Justice for the fairs, from their origins, falls to the king's conservator/guardian. Bourgeois gain arbitrators for fair disputes before royal appeal. This is a precursor to commercial tribunals; in Rouen and Toulouse, it is copied in the Paris royal edict of 1536.
The governor
Capetian-created provincial governments administer military affairs in the king's absence, mainly for territorial defense. The Lyonnais governor controls the current Rhône/Loire, plus parts of Velay and Dombes. He oversees three: Lyonnais county, Beaujolais lordship, Forez county.
Post-bailiff/seneschal; predecessors fade. First: Tanneguy IV du Chastel 1462–1468 succeeding seneschals. Broad royal delegation: vice-roy provincial, lieutenant general title.
Functions and powers
The main military responsibility is command of provincial troops; this role diminishes as borders shift. The governor retains authority over strongholds, fortifications, munitions, and troops. A key duty is the discipline of armed men—garrisons are billeted on civilians and often commit exactions.
He is also responsible for public order and calm; civil powers grow in response to disturbances such as brawls or revolts. He deals with general crises (famines and epidemics) and specific matters (roads, circulation, and food regulation).
He mobilizes both royal and municipal forces, including the militia, and can raise the ban and arrière-ban.
Position and support
The office is usually held by members of the high nobility who are loyal to the king and battle-hardened. The role is multifunctional and requires frequent missions; a lieutenant is appointed to act in the governor's absence.
Renaissance role
During the Renaissance Lyon lies near several threats: Savoy's holdings in Bresse, Bugey, and Gex, with their ambiguous policy; Burgundy, the enemy during the Hundred Years' War and occupied in the Mâconnais by Charles the Bold; and the Habsburg Franche-Comté bordering the Holy Roman Empire.

The finance bureau
Lyon's finance bureau is created in 1578 along with others in the kingdom.
* 1577 reform: tax rationalization, pragmatically new offices/revenues.
* Scope: Generality of Lyon.
* Five members inaugural June 9, 1578 Roanne Palace: ex-France treasurers Camus brothers, Groslier, de l'Aulbe; newcomer Garrault, Épargne treasurer.
Early: treasurers' homes; 1582 rent Rue Saint-Jean house.
Foreign nations
Renaissance Lyon attracts large foreign communities of artisans, merchants, and bankers. By the early 16th century they are so numerous that native Lyonnais regard the city as cosmopolitan, as noted by Symphorien Champier: "Where dwell folk of all nations, as Italians, Florentines, Genoese, Lucchese, Allobroges, Germans, Spaniards and others."
Sufficiently large and structured groups form "nations." Their influx is encouraged by letters patent of Charles VII in 1420 (later renewed), which grant tax exemptions to French and foreign merchants. They organize and regulate their members and represent them to local authorities, the consulate, the king, or their places of origin.
The nations are regular interlocutors of the consulate and staunchly defend their privileges. Their representatives participate in solemnities, especially royal and grand entries. Confident in their wealth and power, they display their fortune through rich equipages and clothing of silk, velvet, and silver. As one visitor observed: "By commerce, men, women, aspect, this city echoes beautiful Italy, making it France's fairest."
The Italians constitute the most numerous and important nations from the origins of the fairs to the end of the Renaissance. They originate mainly from Florence, Milan, Genoa, and Lucca, with smaller numbers from Bologna and Venice.
Florentine nation
The wealthiest and most numerous of the Lyonnais nations is the Florentine. Notable families include the Gadagne, the Medici, and the Capponi. Like great clans, they welcome political exiles. They dominate for a century from the mid-15th to the mid-16th; thereafter they gradually withdraw, though retaining key posts such as Lyon customs.
They have an officially structured constitution, revised and approved by Florence. The first known version dates to 4 January 1477 (though an earlier one may have existed around 1447 in Geneva). It is reformed on 11 July 1501 to strengthen ties with the Florentine Republic. The leaders at this reform are Nicola del Bene, Thomas I de Gadagne, and Giovanni Vecchietti.

The leadership consists of four counsellors and one consul. The consul directs payments at the closing of each of the four annual fairs. Internally, quarterly meetings defend Florentine privileges and freedom of commerce and ensure adherence to the law and avoidance of scandals. There are always five officers (replacements if absent). Meetings are held at the Saint-John-the-Baptist chapel in Notre-Dame-de-Confort Church.
Key consuls include the banker Nicolas del Bene in 1502, Thomas I de Gadagne in 1505, Jacopo Nardi in 1512, Leonardo Spina in 1541, Lorenzo Capponi in 1556, Francesco Capponi in 1570, Bernardo del Barbigia in 1579, Francesco Martelli in 1583, and Matteo Bartolomei in 1584. By the late 16th century their power wanes and key families depart.
Notre-Dame de Confort Church serves Florentine worship from the earliest times. In 1464 they obtain burial privileges and fund its enlargement and embellishment.

Genoese nation
The Genoese nation is well-established, using elaborate legal structures that separate personal assets from those of the trading company. Companies are rarely familial and usually consist of unions of several lineages.
They are fewer than the Florentines but more numerous than the Lucchese. A tradition of mutual aid exists: Lucchese merchants often handle business for absent Genoese.
They form a formal nation with consuls, treasurers, and counsellors. Conflicts with Charles V exile several families; some obtain French naturalization to settle permanently in Lyon.
Close ties exist between Genoese and Lyonnais merchants, with many Lyonnais firms active in Genoa. Political clashes lead to periodic expulsions: the Genoese expel subjects of the French king in 1496–1500, 1512–1515, and 1529–1535. Retaliatory expulsions occur, but commercial exchanges continue. The main trade is in fabrics—Genoese velvets are sent to Lyon, while Lyonnais, English, and Flemish cloth is sought in Genoa. They also serve first as intermediaries and later as manufacturers in the silk trade.
Flemish nation
Consisting mainly of artists, the Flemish nation is less significant than the Italian ones but exerts considerable artistic influence in painting and engraving. Many pass through Lyon en route to study in Italy; some settle permanently. More than twenty-two artists settle along the banks of the Rhône and Saône. The community is centerd on the Rue Mercière, where Guillaume II Le Roy, Jean de Crane, Liévin Van der Meer, and Mathieu d'Anvers are active. The most prominent member is Corneille de Lyon, who resides on the Rue du Temple.
Political life
From Charles VII to Francis I, the city saw its institutional structure undergo a major transformation. From a prosperous medieval commune whose freedoms were generally respected by the king, it became an international commercial center under close royal control, while its elite became fully integrated into the consolidating monarchical system. From the late 15th century onward, Lyon was drawn into conflicts among the major European powers, and the resulting influx of wealth led to significant evolution in its political organization.
The birth of the fairs and the city's transformation
In the second half of the 15th century, Lyon experienced rapid expansion owing to several favorable circumstances. Charles VII's conflict with Burgundy prompted him to grant Lyon the same privileges as the fairs of Brie and Champagne in 1420 and to establish two annual fairs in 1422. Initially modest, these fairs expanded considerably from the 1460s, transforming Lyon from a regional center into one of Europe's leading commercial and financial hubs.
Charles VII and integration into the kingdom
Around 1445, midway through Charles VII's reign, the city underwent a significant change. At that time the écorcheurs—bands of mercenaries—left the region after being summoned by the king to campaign in Alsace with his son, the future Louis XI, as part of a broader effort to remove these companies from the kingdom. On their return they were subject to the Grandes Ordonnances, which regulated and gradually suppressed their activities.
In 1444 the fairs resumed with strong royal support: a third annual fair was authorized, and merchants of the kingdom were forbidden to attend those in Geneva. Around the same time Jacques Cœur invested heavily in silver mines in the nearby mountains and formed partnerships with local notable families such as the Jossarts and Syvrieus; some of these families, including the Baronnats, later profited from his disgrace. The period saw a strong revival of economic activity in the Lyonnais.
From this point relations between the Lyonnais commune and the monarchy changed. Peace allowed the king to impose greater control over the urban elite through regular taxation and a permanent garrison. The consulate surrendered financial autonomy and influence over major appointments, but this was compensated by the integration of bourgeois figures into royal circles, which secured them desirable local offices. At the same time the 1447 reform of the consulate restricted membership to the wealthiest citizens, excluding the laboring classes and ending general assemblies.
Lyon between Charles VII and Dauphin Louis
Relations with the crown were distinctive between 1447 and 1457 while the dauphin Louis—the future Louis XI—was in exile in the Dauphiné. He visited Lyon on 7 January 1447 before entering the Dauphiné on 15 January. Initial relations were cordial, but Louis's ambitions created tensions, although the Lyonnais bourgeoisie remained loyal to Charles VII. Between 1455 and 1460 they secretly sent the dauphin 3,000 gold écus annually through clandestine messengers.
The situation became more complicated as conflict between father and son intensified. Louis's unauthorized marriage in 1452 to Charlotte of Savoy provoked a strong royal response in the region. Duke Louis I of Savoy negotiated a rapid settlement that left Lyon unaffected. In 1453 royal agents—Marshal de Lohéac, Admiral de Bueil, and Jacques de Chabannes—inspected the city's defenses and transferred command of Pierre Scize castle from the Sire de Beaujeu (Aymard) to Jacques de Lavieu, Sire de Fougerolles.
When Charles left in 1454, Louis retaliated by ravaging royal lands at Valbonne and Montluel. The response was immediate: Antoine de Chabannes encamped troops between Saint-Priest-en-Velin and Saint-Symphorien-d'Ozon in November. The king seized the castles of Rochetaillée, Saint-Bernard, and Genay, staying first at Yvours castle in Irigny and then at Saint-Priest. Over the next two years (1454–1457) he incorporated the Dauphiné into the royal domain and asserted control over the Franc-Lyonnais against Savoyard claims before departing in 1457.
On 25 July 1461—three days after Charles VII's death—Jean de Villeneuve and two delegates were sent to pledge Lyon's loyalty to Louis XI at Genappe before the official news reached him.
The rise of Lyon under Louis XI
Under Louis XI, Lyon avoided the reductions in municipal autonomy imposed on cities such as Angers, Amiens, Bourges, and Poitiers. Taxation and the appointment of officials remained relatively independent. Like Caen and Rouen, the king favored its prosperity and supported the fairs in return for consistent loyalty and prompt payments. Lyon maintained royal favor through embassies bearing gifts, and numerous Lyonnais in the royal entourage advocated on the city's behalf.
This loyalty was evident during the War of the Public Weal. While Archbishop Charles II de Bourbon and his uncle, the Bishop of Le Puy, joined the rebellion, Lyon gave full support to the king.}}
Lacking a standing army, Lyon supplied logistical support—money, provisions, and weapons—to the royal forces, including the Milanese contingent of Galeazzo Maria Sforza. While prudently refusing him entry to the city, Lyon facilitated his plundering in the Forez. Militarily, it contributed a modest company of franc-archers to all campaigns. The king ordered improvements to the fortifications and sent lieutenants to supervise the work.
Unlike other opponents, Louis reconciled with the archbishop, obtaining the legation of Avignon for him in 1472 through Pope Sixtus IV (legate: Cardinal Bessarion; an embassy had been sent to Pope Paul II in 1466 with Thibault de Luxembourg). Charles, more diplomat than prelate, was consecrated in Lyon, confirmed communal privileges, and subsequently served at court. Louis settled disputes in the city's favor against ecclesiastical authorities, including the Saint-Jean chapter (1477 Grenette hall incident). This favoritism, largely fiscal in motivation, extended to granting privileges for silk-working to compete with Italian luxury goods; wary of offending Italian partners, the consuls delayed implementation and financed the relocation of workers to Tours.
Between 1461 and 1476 Lyon served as a rear base for operations against the Duchy of Savoy during the wars in Burgundy. Constantly vigilant against Burgundian and Savoyard threats—frequently closing the gates and conducting espionage—the city experienced heightened tension after the 1468 alliance between Philip II of Savoy and Charles the Bold. It emerged unscathed, and after 1476 benefited from Louis's guardianship over the young Duke Philibert I and control of Savoy through the arranged marriages of the children of the late Yolande of France.
Louis made an extended stay in Lyon in 1476 (March–July). Lodging not at the cathedral chapter (except on 1 June at the Fourvière Chapel), but in the house of the bourgeois Jacques Caille, he managed Italian affairs and the war of Charles the Bold against the Swiss, receiving news of the Battle of Morat on 24 June—just two days after the event—through efficient couriers.|group=note}} This led to the creation of a postal relay system the following year, marking the beginning of modern communication. He also attempted to convene a general council in Lyon, welcomed the legate Giuliano della Rovere on 15 June, and hosted René I of Anjou from 4 May to 9 June to resolve the succession in Provence and Anjou. Foiling plots, he imprisoned Duke Jacques de Nemours in a large iron cage at Pierre Scize before transferring him to the Bastille. Louis returned briefly in May 1482 after a pilgrimage to Saint-Claude.
Under Louis XI consular elections proceeded without incident. The consulate included officers (Grants, Paterins) and bankers (Villars, Baronnats) but no Italians despite their growing prominence. Oversight of the trade masters was absent, and general assemblies ceased. Day-to-day administration was routine, punctuated by embassies sent to secure royal favor or negotiate contributions.
In Italian affairs the king's ally Lorenzo de' Medici maintained an agent in Lyon. When Lyonnet de Roussy was arrested in 1472 on suspicion of Genoese intrigues, Louis intervened on behalf of "my compère." On 14 May 1484 Louis wrote from Lyon to Lorenzo.
In Louis XI's final years (1480–1483) Lyon faced heavy financial demands for the upkeep of the army, principally for the annexation of Burgundy and the repopulation of Arras. After the Battle of Guinegatte in 1479, army modernization included the creation of the Picardie bands at Pont-de-l'Arche. Lyon paid in these years as much as during the entire previous reign. The peak of taxation in 1482 represented the high point of royal fiscal pressure for generations. The city's prosperity nonetheless continued. Louis XI died on 30 August 1483.

Charles VIII
Following Louis XI's death in 1483, regent Anne de Beaujeu attempted to curtail Lyon's privileges in favor of other royal cities that had become economically stagnant. In 1484, however, these privileges were restored at the request of Charles VIII, who required substantial funds for his projected Italian campaign. The regent nevertheless promoted the fairs by developing a new route from Moulins to Lyon via Tarare, using river barges on the Loire in place of the old Roman road.
Charles VIII arrived in March 1494 en route to conquer the Kingdom of Naples, thereby beginning the Italian Wars. The young king remained in the city for five months while persuading his council and organising the expedition. The campaign was financed by Italian bankers and by royal towns; Lyon contributed 10,000 livres in return for confirmation of its four annual fairs.
The expedition left in July; wealthy Lyonnais merchants acted as quartermasters and profited considerably, although some incurred losses. Charles returned in November 1495 and was greeted with elaborate celebrations, but these were quickly followed by new demands for funds for another campaign. In exchange for further subsidies the consuls obtained a patent of December 1495 granting nobility to members of the consulate.
Over the next two years Charles extracted additional funds for a second attempt to reconquer Naples, but he died in April 1498 without achieving it. The grant of nobility and the repeated levies caused popular discontent and repeated accusations that the elite were mismanaging municipal funds.

Louis XII
Louis XII continued the expansionist policy, this time aiming at the Milan. Lyon again served as a staging ground and diplomatic center, accommodating the court, nobility, and ambassadors from 1499 to 1503. The effects of the Italian Wars were twofold: increased royal subsidies against the background of wealth generated by the fairs, and enhanced prestige from hosting prominent figures. In 1498 the king's ally Cesare Borgia was granted the honorary governorship of Lyon, though he never exercised it.
Lyon followed royal fortunes closely. Preparations for the Milan campaign took place in the summer of 1498, followed by celebrations and a commemorative medal on 7 November. Defeats the following year led to regrouping in 1500; subsequent victories brought the captives Ludovico and Ascanio Sforza to imprisonment at Pierre-Scize.
Under Louis, grain shortages in 1501 and 1504–1505 remained relatively mild and caused no major disturbances.
Francis I
Upon his accession in 1515, Francis I prepared a campaign for Milan, basing the government in Lyon with Chancellor Antoine Duprat and the financier general Semblançay. Borrowing 300,000 écus from Lyonnais banks at rates of approximately 16% became the standard method of financing the war. The victory at the Battle of Marignano was celebrated with elaborate festivities.
Returning in 1522 for the Sixth Italian War, Francis learned of the defeat at Bicocca. In 1523 40,000 troops under Guillaume de Bonnivet assembled in the region; Francis arrived on 22 August and waited for the traitor Constable Charles de Bourbon before crossing the Alps. The scale of the plot delayed departure, led to the closing of the city gates, and resulted in arrests, and prompted Charles to advise Charles V to attack Lyon. Provence was invaded instead, but Charles failed before Marseille. Bonnivet led the army into Italy while Francis remained behind.
Royal government in Lyon and the regency
Francis re-entered the city on 7 August 1524 accompanied by his mother Louise of Savoy, his sister Margaret of Navarre, and the court. He passed through quickly, but the government remained for more than fifteen months. Moving on to Provence, he repelled the imperial invasion and retook Milan. The entire state apparatus assembled in Lyon: the King's Council, the Grand Council, Duprat, the clergy, financiers, and diplomats. The court's patronage of humanism stimulated intellectual activity in the city.
News of the disaster at the Battle of Pavia prompted the regent Louise to centralise power and summon Bourbon and additional troops. The remnants of the Italian army returned under the Duke of Alençon (who died in Lyon) and Henry II of Navarre. The consulate hastily strengthened the fortifications despite severe financial constraints.
The 1525 Treaty of Moore—ratified on 21 October—with Henry VIII of England made cities such as Lyon guarantors in the event of royal default. Louise left in February 1526 after the Treaty of Madrid secured Francis's release, a treaty negotiated in part by the future Archbishop Francis de Tournon.
The 1529–1531 grain crisis and the Great Rebeyne of 1529
In April 1529 grain riots broke out amid fluctuating wheat prices and shortages caused by population growth. Placards incited crowds to attack the Cordeliers convent as alleged hoarders. The consulate's inaction led to the pillaging on 25 April of several houses, the Cordeliers convent, the residence of Symphorien Champier, the town hall, and the flour weigh-house. Overwhelmed notables and Lieutenant-General Pomponne de Trivulce (nephew of the absent Governor Teodoro Trivulzio) took refuge in the Saint-Jean cloister. Mobilization of the militia failed because artisans and shopkeepers were excluded from power.
The following day rioters searched for supposed hidden reserves; on 27 April they attacked the abbey on Île Barbe. Royal authorities reasserted control by mobilising the militia. The governor arrested seventeen people; eleven were hanged without delay.
Grain scarcity recurred in 1530 accompanied by plague in April, and again in 1531. Desperate rural poor poured into the city and died in large numbers. Traditional aid through the pennons proved insufficient, and the elite distributed food liberally before establishing the General Alms to assist the able-bodied destitute.

End of Francis I's reign
The 1530s saw several royal processions through Lyon connected with Italian affairs. Notable events included the 1533 entry of Eleanor of Austria accompanied by the Dauphin Francis and the Cardinal-Legate Duprat, and the 1537 marriage of James V and Madeleine of France.
Fearing a possible Alpine offensive by Charles V in 1536, Francis established himself in Lyon to oversee military and diplomatic preparations. While there he learned of the death of his son Francis in August. Suspecting poison, he arrested Count Sebastiano Montecuculli (who had offered the prince water shortly before the onset of illness) and condemned him to be quartered and gibbeted at the city gates. During this stay Francis also granted Piedmontese merchants privileges to practise silk-weaving in Lyon.
In 1539 Lyon experienced the first printers' strike in France—the so-called grand tric—when the griffarins guild halted work for several months in pursuit of better conditions. They achieved little, and subsequent litigation reaffirmed the dominance of the trade masters.
From the 1540s onward French foreign policy shifted toward the north and east, diminishing Lyon's strategic role and reducing the frequency of royal visits. New trade taxes damaged the fairs, particularly the silk sector. Escalating royal financial demands forced the city to adopt innovative and sometimes resisted forms of taxation on the population.

Henry II
Henry II entered the city on 23 September 1548 and was received with an elaborate entry intended to display royal power to the new sovereign. Italian merchants imported artists: the painter Nannoccio della Costa da San Giorgio and the sculptor Zanobi for theatrical performances at the archiepiscopal palace.
Henry's reign saw an expansion of royal administration. Seeking tighter control over the city, he sent commissaires drawn from the Maîtres des Requêtes to the Hôtel de Ville. He increased the staff of the généralité and created a présidial court in 1551, thereby reorganising local finances. These reforms supported an ambitious military policy that exhausted credit by 1555. Henry and his financiers consolidated the debts into the Grand Parti, which remained unresolved; the bankruptcy of 1557 severely damaged Lyonnais bankers, many of whom either left the city or scaled back their operations.
Wars of Religion in Lyon
, 16th century, collections of the Musée Gadagne.|left]]
Toward the end of Henry II's reign, during the 1550s, tensions leading to the Wars of Religion escalated across France and in Lyon. The city was directly affected from the conflict's outset by the Protestants' seizure of power in 1562 and the violent actions of Baron des Adrets. This brief episode, though intense, was less destructive than events in many other parts of France. It was not until the 1570s, with the so-called "Lyonnais vespers", that the city experienced severe internal conflict, resulting in a large-scale exodus of Protestants.
Rise of tensions
In the 1550s friction intensified between uncompromising Catholics and the consulate. The latter sought to maintain independence and religious tolerance in order to protect the fairs, which were essential to the city's prosperity.
Following the 1551 Edict of Châteaubriant, Archbishop François de Tournon and the judicial authorities pursued repressive measures that were frequently opposed by the consulate and the seneschal's court. Nevertheless, several arrests and executions took place, including that of the minister Claude Monier in 1551 and of five students from Lausanne in 1552. Around a dozen executions occurred during the decade, heightening tensions without preventing the spread of Reformed ideas.
In 1559–1560 Protestants armed themselves throughout France, forming companies and attempting to seize cities or engaging in clashes with Catholics—for example, Charles Dupuy-Montbrun's attempt in the Comtat Venaissin or Paul de Mouvans's actions in Provence. In this context the Protestants made their first attempt to take Lyon in September 1560, but the plot was foiled by Lieutenant Antoine d'Albon acting for Governor Jacques d'Albon de Saint-André. organized by Edme de Maligny during a fair and supported by Calvin, the conspirators infiltrated the city disguised as merchants. When discovered, Antoine d'Albon's arquebusiers engaged them on the Rue Longue; the Protestants were repelled and fled the following day along with compromised local supporters. Governor Jacques d'Albon hurried to the city and imposed severe repression.
The archbishop, who was highly active, summoned preachers and arranged for the printing and distribution of French-language books of piety and devotional images. This vigorous proselytism increased the charged atmosphere. During the Corpus Christi procession on 5 June 1561 a young Protestant who desecrated the host was lynched by the crowd; the disturbance rapidly escalated, with assaults on Huguenots and the killing of the suspected heretic Barthélemy Aneau.
The regent Catherine de' Medici's national policy of appeasement also applied to Lyon. Lieutenant Antoine d'Albon, regarded as excessively harsh, was replaced by François d'Agoult, Count of Sault. The consulate, seeking compromise, admitted two Reformed members in December 1561: the bookseller Henri de Gabiano and the silk merchant Guillaume Henry.
1562: Lyon as a Protestant city
Nationwide, Protestants armed themselves fearing repression and either defended or seized cities. Attempts took place in Tours, Blois, Poitiers, Bourges, Sens, Angers, and elsewhere. Many failed and strongholds were quickly retaken by royal troops. The Protestant takeover of Lyon occurred within this broader movement.
Seizure and organization of power
Tensions reached their peak when rumors of an approaching Catholic army mobilized the local Protestants. Overnight on 29–30 April 1562 they seized the main strategic points: the town hall, the squares, the bridges, and the gates. By dawn only the lieutenant-general d'Agoult and the canons of Saint-Jean offered brief resistance. The canons fled the following night and d'Agoult surrendered on 1 May. The Protestants kept him in office and proclaimed their loyalty to Charles IX, claiming they acted to free him from the influence of the Guise family.
To maintain control in a predominantly Catholic city they called on the Baron des Adrets, an ally of Condé, for military assistance. He rapidly organized defenses and requested Swiss support. To secure supplies he took Reformed communities in Belleville, Mâcon, and Chalon by force. Criticized for the atrocities committed by his troops—even by fellow Reformed—he was arrested on 10 January 1563 for negotiating surrender with the Duke of Nemours and remained imprisoned until the end of the Protestant occupation.
The Protestants preserved a legal façade while holding real power. An extraordinary assembly on 7 May 1562 added twelve new consuls without removing the Catholic incumbents, temporarily increasing the total to twenty-four in order to maintain appearances. Several Catholic consuls went into exile, while actual decisions were taken by parallel bodies: a consistory of exemplary Protestants who handled all matters and a council of the Reformed Church that liquidated seized ecclesiastical property and paid ministers.
Protestant actions in Lyon
The most visible action was a wave of iconoclasm: all churches were looted and Catholic worship was suppressed. Statues in Saint-Jean Cathedral were destroyed or decapitated; its rood screen and the cloister of Saint-Just were demolished by 23 May. Religious motives predominated, though strategic considerations also played a role—the fortified Saint-Just stood on a promontory that was difficult to defend. Clergy were expelled, Masses prohibited, and attendance at Reformed services made compulsory. The effect on belief is uncertain, but peak communion attendance reached approximately 25,000.
During their short period of control the Protestants carried out extensive urban improvements that reshaped Lyon: major streets were widened, a new ascent to Fourvière was created, the Saint-Jean walls were breached to allow north-south passage, a Peninsula route aligned with the Guillotière bridge was opened (Rue Bellecordière), Rue de Clermont was driven through the Saint-Pierre abbey enclosure, the Lanterne ditches were filled to form the future Place des Terreaux, etc. These works were primarily functional and derived from long-discussed projects; none were reversed by the later Catholic consulates.
Economically the Protestant consulate faced the collapse of commerce, which drastically reduced revenue while expenditure on works and defense soared. The fairs ceased and foreign merchants and bankers fled. Rents and taxes went unpaid and soldiers demanded prompt wages under threat of pillage. Without the relief provided by trade, the inhabitants bore heavy burdens and the consulate accumulated a debt that progressively constrained the city.
The queen appointed the Duke of Nemours governor of the Lyonnais on 27 December 1562, but the consuls rejected him as an enemy. They asked Condé to send a lord to restrain des Adrets' troops; he sent Jean de Parthenay-Larchevêque, Lord of Soubise. Soubise put an end to the excesses of des Adrets, prioritised defense against Nemours, and assumed the governorship of Lyon. The queen demanded his resignation, which he refused. He defeated Nemours and forced his withdrawal.
End of Protestant power
Lyon's fate was determined by national events, which quickly turned against the Protestants. Prince Condé's failure at Dreux doomed the Huguenot uprisings; Catherine de' Medici demanded Soubise's submission and threatened the destruction of Lyon. Protestant leaders resisted for six months but were disappointed by the terms of the Edict of Amboise in March 1563.
Emissaries negotiated with the queen mother and obtained the removal of the hated Nemours, who was replaced by Marshal de Vieilleville. An assembly of notables on 9 June accepted the conditions, the most difficult of which was the return of ecclesiastical property. The marshal entered the city on 15 June and the Edict of Amboise was proclaimed on 24 June.

Catholic reconquest: 1563–1575
After the Protestant interlude Lyon enjoyed relative confessional calm between 1563 and 1566. Tensions persisted—insults and threats occurred—but no major violence broke out. Protestants were able to hold a national synod in the city in August 1563. Violence subsided with the disbandment of armed bands, a development long awaited by the population.
Under the Catholic governor Vieilleville, however, Protestant emigration began. The Reformed community shrank to 400–500 regular communicants. Vieilleville granted a small concession: contrary to the terms of the Edict of Amboise, two intra-mural temples were authorised, followed by a third.
The plague of 1564, which killed about one-third of the population, provoked a polemical exchange between Catholic preacher Father Edmond Auger and Protestant pastor Pierre Viret. The controversy generated pamphlets printed by Catholic presses (Michel Jove) and Protestant ones (Jean Saugrain). The passage of Charles IX in June–July 1564—organized by the poet and schoolmaster Charles Fontaine—did not calm the situation. The king issued an edict prohibiting Protestant worship inside the city walls and requiring it to take place outside in accordance with the Edict of Amboise. The prohibition was widely ignored; services continued at the temples of Paradis, Bourgneuf (Fleur de Lys), and Terreaux.
Although a parity consulate had been envisaged, from 1564 the king increasingly influenced appointments in favor of loyalists. Only the Reformed consuls protested against the violation of consular liberties, finding no support from their Catholic colleagues. Nevertheless, confessional division among the elite remained incomplete; members of both sides collaborated to reduce tensions and to continue the urban policies initiated under Protestant rule.
The monarchy, considering Lyon unreliable, constructed a citadel ostensibly for the city's protection but intended to house a garrison of loyal troops nearby. Completed in 1565, the Saint-Sébastien citadel accommodated 400 men.|group=note}} The population regarded the fortress as a sign of royal distrust and protested against the demolitions required for its construction.
Peaceful coexistence ended in 1567–1568. All official pastors were expelled. Many Protestants, particularly printers, emigrated—mostly to Geneva. Reformed preaching was suppressed and worship sites were regularly closed. In this climate of rising tension the Protestant community was effectively destroyed on 31 August 1572 in the so-called "Lyonnais vespers".

Triggered by news of the St. Bartholomew's Day massacre, the event resulted in the killing of several hundred Protestants in an enthusiastic Catholic reaction.
The primary cause was the time lag between official news and rumours of the Paris massacre. By 24–25 August travellers and merchants reported the attempted assassination of Coligny on 22 August and the subsequent killings. The governor did not receive the royal letter until the 27th. Popular agitation increased. The governor posted guards at strategic points and published the king's letter calling for calm, temporarily restoring order.
On the evening of the 28th a letter from courtiers at the consulate detailed the killings in Paris from 24–26 August and concluded that the king approved them, implying that Lyon should follow suit. Read in session, the letter circulated quickly and rekindled unrest. The consulate hesitated in the absence of clear orders; Catholic radicals gained the upper hand, two moderates left the meeting, and responsibility for the ensuing massacre fell on the remaining members. They ordered the imprisonment of leading Protestants, ostensibly for their protection. That first night violence broke out and one of the three remaining pastors was killed. The incidents remained relatively contained.
The following day the governor ordered all Protestants to gather under his custody for secure imprisonment by royal troops rather than the urban militia. They were confined in the Cordeliers, Célestins, Roanne palace, and the archiepiscopal prisons on 30 August. Some pillaging and destruction occurred, but violence was limited. On the 31st the governor summoned Lyonnais nobility for assistance; troops arrived late.
For several days radical Catholics incited the populace by claiming that the king had accepted the "purificatory" massacre in Paris and would therefore endorse similar action in Lyon. On the morning of the 31st—with the governor absent suppressing unrest in Guillotière—two consuls, André Mornieu and Guillaume Rouillé, led a procession accompanied by the captain of the militia arquebusiers. At the archiepiscopal prison they conducted sham trials, forcing conversions; those who refused were killed on the spot. Systematic violence moved from prison to prison over that day and the next two. During the first two days (31 August–1 September) the killings were ritualistic: bodies were stabbed by crowds, dismembered, and thrown into the river. The mob regarded the acts as divine justice approved by the king. From 2–4 September the murders became less spontaneous.
The number of dead is unknown but probably ran into the hundreds; with forced conversions, disappearances, and flight, Lyonnais Protestantism was effectively destroyed. All social strata were affected, and the city became an intransigent Catholic stronghold.
Lyon during the Catholic League
Lyon distances itself from the king: 1575–1588
After the 1572 massacres rendered Lyon firmly Catholic, the city displayed no early signs of the ultra-Catholic militancy that would characterize the League. While radical Catholic rebellion began in Paris as early as 1584, the first clear evidence in Lyon dates only to 1588.
Locally, the slide into League allegiance stemmed primarily from royal pressure on the city corporation, above all the military distrust symbolised by the Saint-Sébastien citadel. Officially built to protect Lyon from a Protestant coup, everyone understood it was intended to keep the city under surveillance. After the 1572 "Lyonnais vespers," that justification collapsed, and repeated delegations begged the king to demolish it — without success.
In 1585, royal favorite Jean Louis de Nogaret de La Valette, Duke of Épernon purchased the governorship of the fortress and installed his appointee, the sieur du Passage. The latter behaved with open independence toward the king's lieutenant-general in the Lyonnais, François de Mandelot. Consulate and Mandelot joined forces, raised troops, and seized the citadel on 2 May 1585 while arresting du Passage in the city itself. A delegation then demanded once more that Henry III destroy the now-royal-controlled stronghold. The king agreed in exchange for 40,000 écus compensation; the demolition took place amid general rejoicing.
This action demonstrated Lyon's willingness to oppose the sovereign militarily if necessary. At the same time, League ideas circulated ever more widely. Recurrent plague and grain shortages kept the populace agitated while Archbishop Pierre d'Épinac and Governor Mandelot, with consulate support, formed a sworn armed association against Protestants — and against overly moderate Catholics, especially Épernon. Radical sentiment was further revealed in the city's 1588 cahier de doléances sent to the Estates-General at Blois, which closely echoed the extremist positions of Paris.
Lyon as a League city: 1588–1594
Like many French cities, Lyon joined the League after the assassination of Henry, Duke of Guise and his brother Cardinal Louis de Lorraine at Blois on 23 December 1588.
Anger increased when the king imprisoned both the archbishop and Governor Mandelot. Hesitation ended when rumour spread that Épernon was marching on Lyon with an army. The consulate mobilized the pennonage militia and put the city on war footing. On 25 February 1589 it declared that the murder of the Guises released Lyon from allegiance to a regicide king and demanded Henry III dismiss his advisers and adopt uncompromising Catholic policy.
On 2 March 1589 the municipal authorities swore allegiance to the Holy League. Royalist partisans were exiled and a dual military–civilian government established: the consulate assisted by a Council of the Holy Union, flanked by Archbishop Pierre d'Épinac and the new governor, Charles-Emmanuel de Savoie-Nemours (half-brother of the archbishop).
The political upheaval produced considerable intellectual activity. Scholars published treatises and placards justifying or condemning the act of deposing a king for religious reasons. Between 1589 and 1590 Lyon's presses issued more than 280 works on the subject, the most prominent authors being Pierre Matthieu, Claude de Rubys and André de Rossant.
The alliance quickly fractured over divergent interests. Nemours, closely tied to the House of Savoy, pursued a separatist project aimed at annexation by his cousin Charles Emmanuel I of Savoy. In April 1589 he reformed city government to favor his noble allies. Archbishop and consulate drew together, unwilling to embark on a Savoyard adventure.
The League regime imposed heavy taxation to finance war against Henry III (now Henry IV after 1589). Coming when Lyon was already impoverished by decades of religious conflict, these levies encouraged royalist subversion and alienated local power centers. Nemours even contemplated creating his own principality from Lyonnais, Forez, Beaujolais, Auvergne, Bourbonnais and La Marche.
On 21 September 1593 an insurrection led by the consulate expelled Charles-Emmanuel de Savoie-Nemours. No League leaders were executed, but more than sixty ringleaders were banished.
Financial difficulties and institutional disorder
Caught between collapsing fair revenues and heavy military expenditure, the city's finances collapsed. For 1594 alone, Henri Hours records a debt exceeding 630,000 écus — only Paris and Marseille were more indebted in France at that time. One symptom was the proliferation of low-denomination counterfeit or debased coinage that authorities struggled to suppress. To sustain such debt, consuls were forced to assume ever-larger personal shares, passing the burden to successors and making it difficult to find candidates willing to serve.
This partly explains the distortion of normal consular elections: in the absence of volunteers, outgoing consuls were simply re-elected year after year, breaking centuries-old custom.

During the Renaissance, Lyon found itself at the heart of the first wave of globalization, propelled by two converging phenomena: the reconfiguration of European trade in the 15th century and the establishment of the famous Lyon fairs.
At the end of the Hundred Years' War, north-western Europe, including France, lay exhausted by continual warfare and heavy taxation. From the early 15th century onward, the axis stretching from Swabia to northern Italy profited from its rivals' weakness and enjoyed sustained economic growth. This route was paralleled by another major trade corridor running from north-eastern Europe to the Iberian Peninsula, benefiting German and northern Italian cities alike. When the Kingdom of France recovered after several decades of relative peace around 1450, Lyon emerged at the center of a new economic space.
This space became polarised along the Rhône and Saône valleys once the fairs established by Charles VII in 1420 gained momentum after mid-century. From the 1460s they experienced rapid success, transforming Lyon from a modest frontier town of little importance into one of Europe's leading economic centers for more than a century.
For Lyon, the four annual fairs were a major source of revenue. The city participated fully in the major European trade currents and benefited from the near-absence of guilds: most trades were practiced freely, without restrictive regulations. This environment allowed industries—above all printing and textiles—to develop very rapidly.
The fairs and long-distance trade
Lyon owed its considerable prosperity and full participation in the Renaissance to its fairs, which quickly attracted merchants and bankers from across Europe.

Creation and early difficulties
The two annual fairs created in 1422 had been suspended in 1429 because of marauding Écorcheurs, but were revived in 1444. The following year Charles VII added a third and forbade French merchants from trading at Geneva in order to favor Lyon's growth. Immediately after his accession, Louis XI confirmed the privileges on 7 October 1461. Foreign and French merchants had enjoyed tax exemption at the fairs since 1420.
Letters patent of 8 March 1463 authorized a fourth fifteen-day fair, accompanying the fairs' rapid expansion. They now lasted sixty days per year instead of nine.
Paradoxically, the fairs were threatened by French goods themselves. On 20 October 1470 Louis XI convened representatives of the kingdom's merchant cities at Tours to curb the outflow of bullion, since large quantities of foreign merchandise entered France via Lyon. When attempts at Caen and Rouen failed, the merchants asked the king to suppress the Lyon fairs in favor of Norman ones. Louis XI refused and upheld Lyonnais rights.
Other powers also tried to undermine Lyon. The Burgundian-controlled fairs at Chalon-sur-Saône were one rival; in Savoy, Amédée IX forbade merchants to attend Lyon on 25 September 1465 in retaliation for Louis XI's ban on Geneva. Conferences at Montluel in 1467 eventually granted two fairs per year to each city on staggered dates, provoking outrage in Lyon. On 14 November 1467 Louis XI annulled the agreement and restored Lyon's four fairs.
The death of Charles the Bold in 1477 significantly changed the competitive landscape. As Geneva's fairs declined (burdened by heavy fines owed to the Swiss), Lyon's expanded considerably, becoming one of Europe's principal commercial and financial centers. After 1494 the fairs' existence was never again seriously challenged.

Organization
The four fairs opened on the first Monday after Epiphany (Foire des Rois''), the Sunday after Quasimodo (Easter fair), 4 August, and 3 November (All Saints' fair). Each lasted fifteen days, during which no cash changed hands; merchants simply recorded agreements in ledgers.
Payments followed in three stages. First, merchants met under the leadership of the Florentine nation's consul to accept or protest previous deals. Two to four days later came the "exchange" phase, fixing payment dates, interest rates, and foreign-exchange rates. Three days after that, final settlement occurred in cash, specie, or bills of exchange. Many merchants "cleared" debts by offsetting them against others present, a system close to modern clearing.
Location
Early on, the consulate tried alternating fairs between the "kingdom" (right) and "empire" (left) banks of the Saône, but Louis XI eventually ordered merchants left free to gather where they wished. The whole city became a vast European marketplace, with traders grouping by nationality or affinity.
Fairs spilled across shops, streets, trestles, and the ground, centerd on the Saône bridge. On the kingdom side they stretched from the Juiverie quarter to Place de Roanne; on the empire side from Place de l'Herberie (modern Place d'Albon) via Rue Saint-Éloi, Rue Mercière, and the quarters of Platière, Grenette, Saint-Antoine, and Cordeliers to the Rhône. Over time they extended to Place du Confort and Les Terreaux.
Merchants also rented street-front shops, which doubled as warehouses. Specific trades gradually clustered: furriers first in Rue Juiverie, later at Grenette and Cordeliers; haberdashery near Saint-Nizier and on the bridge; hardware at Place du Confort.
Goods traded
At its economic zenith Lyon handled a large volume of art objects. The city was "the most important marketplace for works of art, precisely because of the large presence of Italian trading companies" ("''le plus important marché d'œuvres d'art, précisément à cause de la forte présence des compagnies commerciales italiennes"). The Lyonnais branch of the Capponi family supplied marble statues to Constable Anne de Montmorency, sculptures for the villa of Beauregard, and a marble fountain to Anne de Beaujeu.
Lyonnais merchants
Lyonnais merchants actively participated by travelling abroad. Several families sent agents to Genoa to sell English or Flemish cloth and local products while importing silk. They never formed a formal "nation" in Genoa (unlike foreigners in Lyon) and suffered when French kings expelled Genoese merchants during conflicts, though they successfully resisted Genoese taxation attempts such as the Drictus Sabaudie (1508–1511).
Many Lyonnais families—Camus, Faure, Malezieu—built the foundations of an active early capitalism.
Landownership by the Lyonnais bourgeoisie
Enriched Lyonnais bourgeois became substantial landowners, strengthening their social position at the expense of traditional lords (archbishops and canons).
The 1493 nommées'' (tax rolls) show 849 taxpayers owning c. 1,900 hectares outside the city, concentrated west of Lyon along the rivers (Vaise to Millery), with significant holdings in the hills of Tarare, Jarez, and the slopes of Pilat. The figures are certainly understated, as the rolls omitted the Monts d'Or and the Irigny–Vernaison area where Lyonnais elites had long been heavily implanted.
Vineyards accounted for 55% of rural investment; the wealthiest concentrated on livestock. During crises, bourgeois lent money to village communities, bought produce, and invested in mills, irrigation, and buildings, especially in the second half of the 15th century. Many also purchased simple annuities or rents in kind, which became commonplace during the Renaissance.
Silk in Lyon
Silk manufacturing appeared in Lyon during the Renaissance. Favored by the fairs, entrepreneurial freedom, and frequent royal presence, the industry grew rapidly, reaching a period of prosperity under Henry II before suffering a severe crisis during the Wars of Religion.

An aborted first attempt
The initiative came from Louis XI's desire to stop the outflow of gold caused by the French nobility's passion for expensive imported (mostly Italian) silk. Letters patent of 23 November 1466 and requests for funding followed in December 1466. A few artisans were brought in, but Lyonnais merchants—fearing to offend Italian partners and drive them to rival Geneva—dragged their feet. The workshops were eventually transferred to Tours in 1470.

Étienne Turquet and the true birth of Lyonnais silk
The successful establishment came with Piedmontese Étienne Turquet and Bartholomé Naris, who obtained royal privilege in October 1536 under Francis I to manufacture cloth of gold, silver, and silk. The consulate actively supported the project, providing premises and cheap labor from charitable institutions. Raw silk duties were lifted, and foreign workers were exempted from taxes.
The first golden age of Lyonnais silk
Success was rapid. By Henry II's 1548 entry, 459 master weavers paraded; 800–1,000 people lived from silk. Production focused on plain fabrics (satin, taffeta, velvet, cloth of gold/silver); patterned silks remained an Italian monopoly until c. 1600.
Silk dominated the fairs: in 1569 it accounted for over half the total value of goods traded.
