1560–1590: the first silk crisis
The Protestant occupation of 1562–1563 triggered an initial shock, followed by plague and, crucially, Charles IX's 50% duty on raw-silk imports. Lyonnais silk lost competitiveness against cheaper (often smuggled) foreign production. Rival cities (Geneva, Besançon, Turin, Milan, etc.) attracted unemployed Lyonnais workers. Loom numbers collapsed from c. 3,000 in the late 1550s to roughly 200 in the 1570s.
The art of the book in Lyon
During the Renaissance, Lyon ranked among Europe's leading centers of book production. Together with Paris it accounted for roughly 90% of all books printed in France in 1530. Originating with German typographers, the trade was quickly taken over by local craftsmen supported by merchants who quickly adopted the new technology. At its peak Lyon had dozens of printers and booksellers and participated fully in the major intellectual currents of the age. Although printing suffered severely in the economic crisis of the later 16th century, bookselling families generally weathered the storm.
Origins of printing in Lyon
The first book printed in Lyon was produced in 1473 by Guillaume Le Roy (German: Wilhelm König) in the workshop of the Lyonnais merchant Barthélemy Buyer, who had brought him from Liège. Buyer developed the business, targeting two markets: jurists (with heavy legal tomes) and cultured elites with religious works, chivalric romances, practical medicine, and vernacular texts. He opened branches in several French cities and exported to Italy and Spain, contributing to Lyon's later success in printing.
From the outset the Lyonnais printing milieu was highly cosmopolitan. The fairs and tax exemption until 1495 attracted foreigners, especially Germans and French provincials; few native Lyonnais appeared in the earliest decades.
Characteristics of Lyonnais publishing
Lyon became a major European printing center. The fairs provided both capital and markets, while the initially loose organization of the trade kept labor costs moderate. German, Venetian, and Florentine printers settled mainly in Rue Mercière and the Saint-Nizier quarter.
The Lyonnais book world was strongly influenced by Venice, especially by Aldus Manutius. Italian humanism and typographic innovations such as italic spread quickly. Leading humanist printers included Sébastien Gryphe, François Juste, Étienne Dolet, and Jean de Tournes. Italian printers such as Giacomo Giunti, Vincenzo Portinari, and Barthassard de Gabiano also established themselves, publishing mainly fellow countrymen.
Within France only Paris rivalled Lyon's output. Paris specialized more in liturgical books and books of hours, but the two cities were closely linked from the start, with no strict specialization. A notable example is Josse Bade, who began as a corrector in Lyon before founding his own press in Paris.
From about a dozen workshops in 1480, Lyon grew to around a hundred by the mid-16th century, supplying an international market aimed chiefly at Spain and Italy. Printers were often scholar-printers who published medicine, romances, and humanist texts alongside the usual religious works; the French Golden Legend appeared as early as 1476.
Most bookseller-publishers did not own presses but commissioned printers. Early on, booksellers were predominantly Italian and printers German, but unlike the great Italian banking dynasties most integrated fully into Lyonnais society.
The most famous was Sébastien Gryphe from Swabia, who produced over a thousand editions and founded a printing dynasty. He trained Étienne Dolet and published Budé, Scaliger, and Politian.
Music printing
Between roughly 1525–1580 Lyon was a major center of music printing, producing sacred, spiritual (including Protestant), and secular music. The leading figure was Jacques Moderne, whose collections such as Motetti del Fiore and Parangon des chansons circulated widely. He was followed by the Beringen brothers, Simon Gorlier, Robert Granjon, Jean de Tournes II, and others. Music printing disappeared from Lyon after c. 1615, ceding entirely to Paris.
The book trades
Renaissance printing required many specialized crafts: type-founders, papermakers (most paper came from Auvergne or Dauphiné), ink-makers, etchers, engravers, and binders. The number of illuminators dwindled, reflecting the shift to printed decoration. In 1545 Lyon had 22 playing-card makers alongside sixty printers and twenty-nine booksellers, evidence of the vogue for cards.
Illumination: the end of an era
Illumination declined during the Renaissance and disappeared around 1530. The last major practitioners were the Master of the Alarmes de Mars, the Master of François I's Entry, and Guillaume II Le Roy, active 1493–1528, who also painted royal entries.
The Wars of Religion and the crisis of the book trade
The religious wars severely damaged Lyon's economy and book trade. Many printers and booksellers emigrated, often to Geneva, in waves (1551 and especially 1567). Geneva offered cheaper provisions and better regulation. Booksellers fared better by having books printed there, but printers collapsed from 63 masters in 1545 to 13 in 1571.
Banking
With the growth of the fairs Lyon became a leading European banking center. From 1466 major Italian houses relocated there: Medici, Bonvisi, Bene, Gondi, Capponi, Salviati, Guadagni (Gadagne). The Gadagne was the largest in the early 16th century, lending heavily to Francis I for the Italian Wars, until absorbed by Capponi in 1556. By 1597 only twenty-one Italian banking houses remained, down from seventy-five in 1568.
Lyonnais merchants also financed early capitalism, notably the pastel boom in Toulouse.
Other sectors
Food trades expanded with population growth; the consulate regulated grain, created public reserves (1549), and moved livestock markets for hygiene. Wine consumption reached approximately 150,000 hectoliters annually.
End of Lyon's prosperity
Lyon's Renaissance period of prosperity ended in the late 16th century. Long-distance trade and banking collapsed between the 1570s and 1590s, accelerated by the 1557 bankruptcy of the Grand Parti de Lyon, the displacement of the fairs during the 1562 Protestant occupation, plague outbreaks in 1564, and general insecurity. The crisis in Antwerp and Philip II's 1557 default further compounded these difficulties.
A major contributing factor was the northward shift of European trade toward England and the Netherlands, along with the development of new Atlantic routes that bypassed Lyon. Many Italian merchant-bankers left the city; local families did not fully replace them, often preferring public offices or investment in rents. The crown provided no sustained fiscal support, and commerce was generally accorded lower social prestige in French society.
Two legacies remained: the fairs continued to play an important role in domestic French trade, and silk manufacturing, introduced in the 1530s, became the city's primary source of economic growth from the early 17th century.
Knowledge and culture
Lyon, during the first half of the 16th century, benefited from a combination of factors that contributed to its prominence in Renaissance humanism in Europe. At that time the city served as France's second capital, with French kings residing there frequently while attending to the Italian Wars. This royal presence supported an existing circle of scholars and poets that included Symphorien Champier, Maurice Scève, and Louise Labé, and attracted courtiers and intellectuals such as the German scholar Cornelius Agrippa, who served as personal physician to Louise of Savoy. The prosperous economy provided support for visiting scholars. The absence of a parliament or university allowed considerable intellectual freedom. In this frontier city, with a strong presence of booksellers, new ideas could be proposed and disseminated more readily than in many other places. Bookselling was the primary means of disseminating Renaissance culture in Lyon. Artistic production, unlike literature, has left few traces, many of which were destroyed by Protestant iconoclasm. Although foreigners commissioned works, the Lyonnais bourgeoisie commissioned few ostentatious pieces.
Foundations of Lyonnais culture
As a frontier city, Lyon developed a culture shaped by its position between several worlds. Lyon lay on the linguistic boundary between Franco-Provençal and langue d'oïl. Throughout the 15th century its elites sought to adopt the culture of their king while continuing to speak the local dialect in daily life. Only around 1460 did official documents begin to be drafted entirely in standard northern French. Despite linguistic assimilation through education, the elites retained a strong local cultural identity, particularly as exchanges with Geneva intensified.
Education
Sources on education in Renaissance Lyon are extremely sparse until the early 16th century. Consular deliberations are almost silent on the subject, tax rolls uninformative, and notarial registers non-existent before 1530. Reconstruction relies on comparison with nearby cities such as Bourg-en-Bresse, Grenoble, and Vienne. In the first half of the 15th century instruction for patrician sons was limited to reading, arithmetic, and basic rhetoric. From the 1460s the situation evolved rapidly: Lyon's growing wealth and network of booksellers attracted qualified teachers (Henri Valluphin, Jean Delorme, Guillaume Ramène, Josse Bade); bourgeois prosperity supported stable schools; civic pride ("the honor of the city") encouraged municipal funding; and humanist and reformist ideals promoted education as the means to regenerate Christian society. By the height of the Renaissance Lyonnais elites had access to every type of school found in major European cities except a university. The most notable institution was the Collège de la Trinité, founded in 1519 by the Confrérie de la Trinité and installed on Rue Neuve. Basic instruction was provided by parish and collegiate churches (e.g. the manécanterie of Saint-Jean). Wealthier families sent children to grammar or law schools or hired private tutors; the richest dispatched sons to prestigious universities.
Festivities and royal entries
In the Renaissance urban elites increasingly sought to distinguish themselves from the populace while presenting increasingly elaborate public displays. Collective festivals became spectacles performed by the bourgeoisie for a passive audience. During mid-16th-century Carnival, wealthy (often Italian) families organized "mommeryes"—lavish processions drawing on classical mythology followed by ring-jousts among notables.
Solemn royal entries
Royal entries allowed the consulate and great families to display wealth and learning through elaborate artistic displays. Under Italian and humanist influence, simple processions evolved into sophisticated scenography rich in classical references. Under Catherine de' Medici esoteric and astrological elements became prominent. Lyon's strategic position during the Italian Wars meant frequent royal visits:

Lyonnais humanism and intellectual life
Lyonnais intellectual life revolved around informal circles of printers, travellers attending the fairs, and members of the royal court.
Fertile ground for humanism
The absence of a university meant printers and scholars worked free from doctrinal oversight. Royal censorship proved impractical given the volume of publications. The early Renaissance archbishop Charles II de Bourbon was an open-minded patron of learning.
The fairs brought Italians and Germans who introduced new ideas; many Italian and German works were translated. Prolonged stays by the court—especially the intellectually open Margaret of Navarre—stimulated encounters among scholars, poets, and philosophers.
Cultural circles
Cultural life centerd on salons hosted by wealthy scholars (Pierre Sala, Symphorien Champier, Guillaume du Choul, Guillaume Scève, Marie-Catherine Pierrevive), printers' workshops (Sébastien Gryphe, Jean de Tournes), and the progressive Collège de la Trinité.
The informal "sodalitium" included passing luminaries such as François Rabelais, Étienne Dolet, Clément Marot, Bonaventure Des Périers, and the brothers Jean and Mathieu de Vauzelles.
Salons included Pierre Sala's gatherings at the Antiquaille (modelled on the Medici academy at Careggi) and Marie-Catherine Pierrevive's salon at the château du Grand-Perron (1520s–1530s), frequented by Dolet, Des Périers, Scève, and others.
Literature
Renaissance Lyon produced an original literary current, free from Parisian censorship and nourished by Italian, classical, and medieval traditions.
Two generations are distinguishable:
* c. 1500: Symphorien Champier and Pierre Sala (the "Académie de Fourvière")
* 1530s peak: Maurice Scève, Louise Labé, Pernette du Guillet, and the anonymous author of the Contes amoureux de Madame Jeanne Flore—known as the Lyonnais school of poetry
The school's love poetry, blending Petrarchism and Neoplatonism, played a pioneering role alongside the Pléiade in the French literary renaissance.
Music

The musical life of Renaissance Lyon remains difficult to quantify and appears more limited than its literary culture or the musical scenes of Paris and the major Italian cities. Frank Dobbins has identified around 150 musicians active in Lyon during the entire 16th century, many of them amateurs and very few publishing their own compositions. Some also worked as instrument makers. The best-known include Guillaume de La Moëlle, Louis Bourgeois, Pierre de Villiers, Philibert Jambe de Fer, Francesco Layolle and his son Alamanno, Eustorg de Beaulieu, François Roussel, Simon Gorlier, and Didier Lupi Second.
These musicians were paid by the consulate or wealthy merchants to perform at civic festivities and royal entries, or to give lessons to affluent families; they usually acknowledged their patrons in printed dedications. Many spent only part of their careers in Lyon, their presence attested solely by the publication of one or more music books.
Church music appears to have been conservative: the canons of Saint-Jean insisted on plainchant and resisted polyphony; almost nothing is known of musical activity in parish churches or collegiate chapels. The only probable exception was the Florentine parish church of Notre-Dame de Confort, where the organist Francesco Layolle collaborated closely with the printer Jacques Moderne.
Lyon was nonetheless an important center of instrument making, especially recorders (Claude Rafi) and lutes (the Tyrolean Gaspard Duiffoprougcar family and their workshop).
Painting and printmaking
Renaissance painting in Lyon is poorly documented. Although production appears to have been abundant, few works survive, owing to destruction during the 1562 Protestant iconoclasm, shifts in artistic taste, and vandalism during the French Revolution.
As a major commercial, banking, intellectual, and political center, Lyon served as a crossroads for European artistic influences. From the late 15th century, its painters incorporated elements from Flemish, Italian, and residual French Gothic traditions. The principal genres were book illustration, exemplified by Bernard Salomon, and portraiture, dominated by Corneille de Lyon.
Official institutions
Only two institutions regulated the visual arts: the position of official painter to the cathedral and the painters' guild.
Cathedral painter
The city's sole official painter position was linked to Saint-Jean. The first holder during the Renaissance was Laurent Girardin (1441–1471), noted for stained-glass windows and a Trinity panel now in Cleveland. His successor (and son-in-law), Jean Prévost (from 1471), undertook varied commissions, including decorations for Louis XI's 1476 entry and paintings for the cathedral clock.
Painters', sculptors', engravers', and glass-painters' guild
In 1496 Charles VIII approved statutes for the guild, whose founding members included the royal painter Jean Perréal. Few works by these artists survive, except for a Saint Catherine attributed to Claude Guinet.
Late 15th century
The expansion of mendicant convents and visits by elite patrons spurred religious commissions. Jean Hey (the Master of Moulins), patronized by Cardinal Charles de Bourbon, worked in Lyon under Louis XI.
First half of the 16th century
Prominent painters included the Master JG (1520s), Corneille de Lyon (from the 1530s), Bernard Salomon, and Jean Perréal. Book illustration developed a characteristic Lyonnais style through Salomon's intricate woodcuts, which drew on Holbein's techniques and Parisian mannerism. The publisher Jean de Tournes helped spread Salomon's illustrations across Europe.
Lyonnais stained-glass painters gained considerable recognition; several worked for the dukes of Savoy at Chambéry.
Second half of the 16th century
Key figures included Maignan, Perrissin, and the printmaker Pierre Eskrich (Woeiriot), whose output illustrates the effects of the religious wars.

Architecture
Italian Renaissance influences on architecture were limited in Lyon. Wealthy foreign residents typically constructed palaces in their home countries, while local elites favored restrained late-Gothic ornamentation. Surviving Renaissance buildings include the church of Notre-Dame de Confort, the Gondi villas at Grand- and Petit-Perron, the Gadagne villa at Beauregard, and Philibert de l'Orme's gallery at the Hôtel de Bullioud.
Italian architects visited the city: Giuliano da Sangallo and Boccador accompanied Charles VIII, while Sebastiano Serlio resided in Lyon from around 1549 to 1554, where he published several volumes of his treatise (including the Extraordinario Libro, which later shaped local preferences).
Sculpture
Foreign communities, particularly Florentines, commissioned sculptures for private use and for Notre-Dame de Confort (including mausolea by Antonio Rossellino and others). Thomas I de Gadagne fitted his Beauregard villa with a rustic nymphaeum.
Faience
Italian potters operated in Lyon from 1512, initially creating pieces similar to those from the Italian peninsula. A recognizably French faience style developed only over time.
Religion in the Renaissance: decline and renewal
During the Renaissance, Lyon was a major European crossroads where almost every spiritual current intersected. From the late-15th-century reconstruction to the Christian humanism of the early 16th century, from the rise of Reformed ideas to the outbreak of the French Wars of Religion, and finally to the Catholic League and subsequent reconciliation, the city experienced every significant religious upheaval of the era.

The late 15th and early 16th centuries were religiously unremarkable periods in Lyon. High church officials, almost always drawn from the nobility and court circles, devoted more attention to royal service than pastoral care. Even before the 1516 Concordat of Bologna formally granted the French king the right to appoint bishops, monarchs had long imposed their choices. Lyonnais archbishops were thus primarily courtiers and diplomats, selected for political utility rather than spiritual leadership. Most held multiple benefices and rarely resided in the diocese.
This absenteeism necessitated a strong administrative apparatus. The archbishop relied on a trusted official, usually a jurist, who presided over the archiepiscopal council and ecclesiastical court in his absence.
Under Cardinal Charles II de Bourbon a pastoral visitation was conducted in 1469–1470, revealing generally satisfactory conditions in parish buildings, liturgical objects, and clerical morals and education. Florentine merchants extensively rebuilt the Jacobin church of Notre-Dame de Confort as their burial place, while Simon de Pavie financed an Annunciation chapel in the Cordeliers' church of Saint-Bonaventure. Charles completed Saint-Jean Cathedral and was buried in its flamboyant-Gothic Bourbon chapel.
Several mendicant orders established houses in Lyon during this period, including the Cordeliers (1467) and Observant Franciscans shortly thereafter.
Early 16th century: humanism and reform
(1537–1539).|left]]
Reformed ideas took root in Lyon during this period, though most early sympathizers sought renewal within the Church rather than schism. Influenced by humanism, the city maintained a degree of confessional ambiguity that delayed open conflict. Until the 1560s religious allegiance often remained fluid.
Archbishops
François II de Rohan (1501–1536), whom historian Henri Hours described as "the best of his era", resided frequently in his diocese and worked to reform clerical abuses. At the 1528 provincial council he condemned Lutheran doctrines and attempted to raise standards among his clergy.
His successors Jean de Lorraine (1537–1539) and Ippolito d'Este (1539–1551) largely neglected the diocese. Commissions for devotional books declined while humanist and proto-Reformed works proliferated.

First signs of new ideas
The earliest traces of reform appear in the 1520s. Bookseller Jean Vaugris requested Lutheran texts from Basel in 1520 and sold works by Erasmus and Lefèvre d'Étaples.
Margaret of Navarre's prolonged stay (October 1524 – August 1525) significantly advanced evangelical sentiment. Surrounded by a court sympathetic to returning to primitive Christianity, she sheltered preachers such as the Dominican Aimé Meigret and the Franciscan Pierre de Sébiville, both of whom were eventually silenced.
At the Florentine church of Notre-Dame de Confort, the Dominican Sante Pagnini worked from 1526 on a new Latin Bible based on Hebrew and Greek sources, supported by Francis I and popes Adrian VI and Clement VII. Though published under Catholic auspices, it belonged to the philological movement that fed Protestant translations.
The first executions for heresy occurred in 1534. Repression intensified in the 1540s but remained milder than elsewhere; a clandestine Reformed congregation of about fifty members formed by 1546.
Spread of Reformed ideas through Lyonnais society
All social strata except Italians were affected by conversions. The fairs brought regular influxes of foreign merchants and ideas; the consulate, jealous of commercial privileges and traditionally hostile to clerical jurisdiction, shielded suspected heretics. The absence of a theology faculty or Sorbonne-like institution left Catholic controversialists without a strong local base. Printers such as the Frellon brothers, Jean de Tournes, Guillaume Rouillé, and Antoine Vincent produced heterodox works alongside orthodox ones.

Late 16th century: religious conflict
Tensions escalated in the 1550s. Despite persecution and exile to Geneva, the number of Reformed adherents grew. The movement emerged as a political force, encouraged by fluctuating royal policy under Catherine de' Medici and the young Charles IX. In 1560 Protestants attempted to seize the city but were defeated by lieutenant-general Antoine d'Albon.
The July 1561 edict granted freedom of conscience, while the January 1562 edict permitted worship outside city walls. By early 1562 over 4,000 attended sermons, and two Protestants entered the consulate.
Lyon as a Protestant capital (1562–1563)
Protestants seized power in April 1562. Churches were stripped of images; Saint-Jean Cathedral and Saint-Just cloister were demolished in an iconoclastic wave that swept much of France.
Religious war (1563–1572)
Catholic restoration relied more on the efforts of individual priests than on archbishops. The Jesuit Edmond Auger preached extensively, ministered to plague victims in 1564, and published a widely circulated catechism. From 1567 the Collège de la Trinité became a Jesuit stronghold.
The Catholic League and final restoration (1572–1595)
Archbishop Pierre d'Épinac (1573–1599) consolidated the Catholic recovery through administrative reforms.
Historiography
The history of Renaissance Lyon has been extensively studied, with dedicated works addressing its political, economic, social, religious, and cultural dimensions. Certain research areas, however, remain underexplored.
Potential research areas
Studies of the consulate could draw on consular deliberations. Available online at the Lyon Municipal Archives: Communication within the city could be examined similarly to work on the 17th century. Fiscal records, exploited only sporadically, and testaments—previously studied by Marie-Thérèse Lorcin for earlier periods—await fuller analysis. Economic and social history is advanced, but monographs on major merchants and their families are lacking, despite surviving traces beyond the destroyed notarial archives. Gaps persist in printing and the arts. Lyon's frontier status remains underexplored.

Historiography of Renaissance urbanism in Lyon
Interest in Lyon's monumental heritage began in the 19th century, with Pierre Martin's 1855 ''Recherches sur l'architecture... dans les maisons du Moyen Âge et de la Renaissance à Lyon. This era produced the Pointet fonds at the municipal archives. From the 1970s, academic work proliferated, including the Documents d'archéologie en Rhône-Alpes et Auvergne series on zones and themes. These reflect broader interest in vernacular archaeology. A first synthesis appeared in 1998 (Pesez and Esquieu). Lyon-specific synthesis followed the 1997 "Au fil du chantier''" exhibition.

Historiography of Renaissance painting
The study of Renaissance painting in Lyon has evolved through distinct phases. The first, contemporary with the artists themselves, consisted of laudatory texts by literati. Jean Lemaire de Belges's 1504 Plainte du désiré praised Jean Hey and Jean Perréal. Early praise focused on portraitists; by mid-century history painters like Bernard Salomon received similar honours.
The 17th–18th centuries saw near-total neglect, except for Salomon and Corneille de Lyon.
From the mid-19th to mid-20th century, local historians revived interest, spurred by collectors such as Pierre Révoil, Jean-Baptiste Carrand, and Édouard Aynard. Key figures included Natalis Rondot, Henri Baudrier, André Steyert, Louis Charvet, Alfred Cartier, and Lucien Bégule, who produced catalogues, repertoires, and dictionaries of Lyonnais artists.
From the 1960s, focus shifted from defining a "Lyonnais school" to situating Lyon in broader European exchanges. The 1965 Petit Palais exhibition Le Seizième siècle européen marked this turn. Recent studies have recontextualized Perréal and Corneille while examining lesser-known figures such as Giovanni Capassini, François Stellaert, and Noël de Lyon. Illumination has been studied by François Avril, Lynn F. Jacobs, and Elizabeth Burin; prints by Peter Sharratt and Vanessa Selbach, including copper engravers (Henri Zerner, Estelle Leutrat).
Legacy
Architectural remnants
Numerous civil and religious buildings from the Renaissance era survive in various quarters of Lyon, particularly in the Vieux Lyon, designated as one of Europe's largest Renaissance districts and inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1998 as part of the Historic Site of Lyon. Notable examples include structures on the Peninsula, such as the Saint-Nizier Church, Lyon, which features a Renaissance portal.
Works of art
Despite losses during the Wars of Religion and subsequent dispersals, surviving Renaissance artworks from Lyon were presented in the 2015–2016 exhibition Lyon Renaissance: Arts and Humanism at the Musée des Beaux-Arts de Lyon, which assembled nearly 300 objects to provide an overview of the city's artistic production during the period.
